items.prompt: What does 'right-sizing' mean in this unit's terms?
choices: Provisioning a resource's capacity to match measured usage plus a deliberate safety margin, instead of a guessed-high number
Trimming every resource down to the smallest instance size available, without checking whether measured usage actually supports that
Provisioning capacity once based on a rough estimate, then treating that number as permanent and never checking it against real usage
A negotiated billing discount some cloud providers apply automatically once a team's monthly compute usage drops below a set threshold
items.explanation: Right-sizing is about matching provisioned capacity to actual, measured usage with deliberate headroom — not blindly minimizing size, and not a provider discount.
items.reference:
📏 Right-sizing = measured usage + deliberate margin
🙈 'Just in case' sizing = guessed margin, never revisited

Why: The gap between a guess and a measurement is where waste hides.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, staging was provisioned for '4x normal load, just in case.' What did measuring actual usage reveal?
choices: Actual peak need was only about 1.2x normal load, meaning the environment was massively over-provisioned
Actual usage occasionally touched 3.5x normal load during scheduled tests, so the original 4x sizing was mostly justified
Usage could only be measured for production, not for staging environments specifically
Staging consistently ran close to its provisioned 4x ceiling, confirming the original guess was reasonable
items.explanation: Once measured, staging's real peak need was around 1.2x normal load — far below the 4x guess used to justify its original sizing, which is exactly the gap right-sizing is meant to close.
items.reference:
📏 Right-sizing = measured usage + deliberate margin
🙈 'Just in case' sizing = guessed margin, never revisited

Why: The gap between a guess and a measurement is where waste hides.

items.prompt: Why is right-sizing described as a loop rather than a one-time exercise?
choices: Because usage patterns drift over time, so a sizing decision made once and never revisited quietly goes stale
Because cloud providers contractually require every resource to be resized on a fixed monthly schedule, per their standard terms of service
Because usage measurements become unreliable after the first time a resource is measured
Because right-sizing was only ever intended to apply to resources in their first month of use
items.explanation: A right-sizing decision reflects usage at the moment it was measured; as traffic, team size, or the product itself changes, the same sizing can become wrong again, which is why re-auditing periodically is part of the loop, not an optional extra.
items.reference:
📏 Right-sizing = measured usage + deliberate margin
🙈 'Just in case' sizing = guessed margin, never revisited

Why: The gap between a guess and a measurement is where waste hides.

items.prompt: Which of L1's three waste sources is 'forgotten test databases' an example of?
choices: Idle/forgotten resources — still running and billing after the project that justified them ended
Unbounded auto-scaling — a scaling group with no ceiling that kept growing after a traffic spike
A billing error on the cloud provider's side that charged for resources nobody actually provisioned
Over-provisioned production sizing — capacity sized above measured peak need from the start
items.explanation: Test databases left running after their project ended are the idle/forgotten resources pattern — capacity nobody is actively using but that keeps billing anyway.
items.reference:
🗑️ Idle/forgotten — still billing after the need ended
🛡️ 'Just in case' — sized above measured need, never revisited
📈 Unbounded autoscale — no ceiling on cost during a spike

Why: Naming the pattern is the first step toward a targeted fix.

items.prompt: A team writes a one-time script that deletes every currently-idle test resource. Six months later, a new batch has accumulated. What did the one-time fix miss?
choices: It resolved the current waste but didn't fix the missing process (ownership, expiry tagging, recurring review) that let idle resources accumulate in the first place
Nothing — a one-time cleanup is sufficient on its own, since idle resources don't realistically tend to reaccumulate once they've already been deleted
The script should have also deleted production resources, since those are just as likely to go idle and unnoticed over time
Idle resources can never actually be prevented in advance, so treating each new batch as a fresh one-time cleanup is the only realistic fix available
items.explanation: Treating idle-resource waste as a single incident to clean up, rather than a recurring pattern to prevent, means the underlying gap (no owner, no expiry, no recurring review) stays open and simply refills over time.
items.reference:
🗑️ Idle/forgotten — still billing after the need ended
🛡️ 'Just in case' — sized above measured need, never revisited
📈 Unbounded autoscale — no ceiling on cost during a spike

Why: Naming the pattern is the first step toward a targeted fix.

items.prompt: What specifically makes 'unbounded auto-scaling' a cost risk, distinct from auto-scaling itself?
choices: Having no upper limit on how far it can scale, so a traffic spike, bug, or retry storm can drive cost as high as the cloud account allows
Auto-scaling is inherently a cost risk even with a sensible ceiling in place, since any scaling event at all adds some unpredictable extra cost
Auto-scaling groups only ever scale down during low traffic, never up in response to a genuine spike
It requires manual approval before every single scaling event, which slows down legitimate traffic responses
items.explanation: Auto-scaling itself is a reasonable, common pattern; the risk is specifically the missing ceiling — without a maximum, nothing stops a spike (legitimate or bug-induced) from scaling cost to the account's practical limit.
items.reference:
🗑️ Idle/forgotten — still billing after the need ended
🛡️ 'Just in case' — sized above measured need, never revisited
📈 Unbounded autoscale — no ceiling on cost during a spike

Why: The ceiling, not the scaling itself, is what needs fixing.

items.prompt: In L1's Scenario, what triggered the auto-scaling group to scale up and stay up?
choices: A retry storm, and it never scaled back down cleanly afterward
A scheduled maintenance window
A deliberate decision to permanently increase production capacity
A billing configuration change made by finance
items.explanation: The Scenario describes an auto-scaling group with no upper bound that scaled up during a retry storm and never scaled cleanly back down, quietly leaving elevated capacity (and cost) running.
items.reference:
🗑️ Idle/forgotten — still billing after the need ended
🛡️ 'Just in case' — sized above measured need, never revisited
📈 Unbounded autoscale — no ceiling on cost during a spike

Why: The ceiling, not the scaling itself, is what needs fixing.

items.prompt: Why did it take a finance invoice, rather than the team itself, to notice the tripled cloud bill?
choices: Nothing was proactively watching total spend the way a dashboard or alert watches a resource metric — cost was only visible retroactively, on the invoice
The team didn't have access to the cloud provider's billing console at all, so nobody could have checked spend even if they'd tried to
The bill tripled in a single dramatic overnight event, one sudden enough that it should have triggered an automatic page to whoever was on call
Finance's internal tooling is inherently more sophisticated at tracking cloud spend than anything engineering could ever build or use
items.explanation: Cost, unlike a CPU spike or an error rate, doesn't page anyone by default — without a deliberately built dashboard, budget, and alert, the running total stays invisible until a bill arrives after the fact.
items.reference:
👀 A resource metric gets watched because someone builds a dashboard for it
🙈 Cost has no such default — it needs the same deliberate tracking

Why: Visibility doesn't happen by accident; it has to be built.

items.prompt: What kind of tooling does this unit say cost visibility needs, to catch a problem before the bill arrives?
choices: The same kind of proactive tracking used for reliability — a dashboard, a budget, and an alert
A stricter manual approval process requiring sign-off before every single cloud resource purchase
Nothing beyond what already exists — invoices remain the correct and sufficient way to track ongoing cost
A quarterly meeting where the team reviews and discusses spending after invoices have already arrived
items.explanation: The unit draws a direct parallel to infra-observability's reliability tracking: a cost dashboard, a budget (the cost equivalent of an SLO), and a proactive alert are what catch a problem while there's still time to act, not a retrospective invoice review.
items.reference:
👀 A resource metric gets watched because someone builds a dashboard for it
🙈 Cost has no such default — it needs the same deliberate tracking

Why: Visibility doesn't happen by accident; it has to be built.

items.prompt: L1 frames the tripled bill as coming from 'three individually-reasonable decisions,' not one dramatic incident. What's the key implication of that framing?
choices: Real cloud waste often compounds from small, unexamined decisions rather than a single obvious mistake, so catching it requires ongoing visibility, not just incident response
Because no single one of the three decisions was individually dramatic on its own, the total $8,400 monthly increase wasn't actually a serious problem worth investigating further
Only large, obviously reckless provisioning decisions made by a careless engineer ever add up to meaningful cloud waste over time
The three decisions were made independently by three completely unrelated teams, so no single review could ever have caught all of them
items.explanation: Small, individually-reasonable over-provisioning decisions, left unexamined and multiplied across many resources and months, is exactly where real cloud bills balloon — which is why ongoing visibility, not a reactive scramble after one big incident, is the actual fix.
items.reference:
➕ Small waste × many resources × long time = a large bill

Why: No single decision has to be dramatic for the total to become one.

items.prompt: Roughly how much of L1's $8,400 monthly increase did the staging-sized-like-production decision account for?
choices: About $3,600/month, the largest single contributor
About $200/month, a negligible amount
All $8,400, with the other two decisions contributing nothing
It's impossible to attribute cost to individual decisions
items.explanation: The staging-sized-like-production decision was the largest of the three contributors at roughly $3,600/month, though all three (staging, forgotten test databases, unbounded autoscale) added up to the full increase together.
items.reference:
➕ Small waste × many resources × long time = a large bill

Why: No single decision has to be dramatic for the total to become one.

items.prompt: Which pair correctly matches a cost-management term to its reliability-tracking counterpart from infra-observability, as this unit frames it?
choices: Budget alert (cost) is the counterpart of a burn-rate alert (reliability) — both catch a problem before a hard limit is actually breached
Right-sizing (cost) is the counterpart of an SLA (reliability) — both are external contractual commitments
Idle resources (cost) is the counterpart of an SLI (reliability) — both are raw measurable signals
There is no meaningful parallel between cost tracking and reliability tracking at all; cost simply has no equivalent of a burn-rate alert
items.explanation: A budget-forecast alert plays the same early-warning role for spend that a burn-rate alert plays for an error budget — both flag a trajectory heading toward a limit while there's still time to act, rather than waiting for the limit to already be breached.
items.reference:
🎯 SLO ↔ Budget (a committed ceiling)
🔥 Burn-rate alert ↔ Budget-forecast alert

Why: The same proactive-visibility shape applies to both axes.

items.prompt: What does this unit mean specifically by 'cost visibility'?
choices: Proactive, deliberate tracking of spend (dashboard, budget, alert) rather than only discovering cost after an invoice arrives
Making a cloud provider's public pricing pages more easily discoverable for customers and engineers alike during planning
A finance team's private internal spreadsheet that tracks spend but isn't shared with the engineering team
The total number of distinct cloud resources a team currently owns across all of its environments

items.reference:
🎯 SLO ↔ Budget (a committed ceiling)
🔥 Burn-rate alert ↔ Budget-forecast alert

Why: The same proactive-visibility shape applies to both axes.

items.prompt: Staging was originally sized for '4x normal load,' and measured usage really did spike to 3.5x normal load once a quarter during a scheduled load test. Does that justify keeping the 4x sizing permanently?
choices: No — the right-sized answer is to provision for typical day-to-day usage and handle the rare, known spike with a temporary scale-up or a deliberate budgeted exception, not by paying for peak capacity year-round
Yes — once a peak has actually been measured, even a rare quarterly one, it justifies provisioning permanently at that level

No, because rare and predictable spikes like a scheduled quarterly load test should simply be ignored entirely and left completely unprovisioned for, since infrequent events don't justify dedicated planning
Yes, because 3.5x measured usage is close enough to the original 4x guess that no sizing change is really needed
items.explanation: Sizing permanently for a rare, predictable event is the same over-provisioning mistake wearing a more defensible-sounding number — the fix is to size for typical usage and handle the known rare spike deliberately (temporary scale-up or a budgeted exception), not to pay for peak capacity all month.
items.reference:
📊 Size to typical usage, not to a rare annual peak
🎯 Handle rare, known spikes deliberately and temporarily

Why: Sizing to the 99th-percentile case forever is over-provisioning with better PR.

items.prompt: A resource's measured peak utilization is 22%. Why does this unit recommend right-sizing toward a target utilization band (e.g. 65%) rather than sizing exactly to the measured 22% peak?
choices: Sizing to the exact observed peak leaves no headroom for a genuine spike above anything previously measured — a target band builds in deliberate margin
The target band is just an arbitrary round number chosen for simplicity, with no real engineering purpose behind it
Sizing to the exact measured peak is always strictly cheaper, so the target band exists mainly to intentionally increase cost
22% utilization is too low a number to be measured accurately by most cloud monitoring tools, so the target band mainly exists to compensate for that error
items.explanation: Trimming a resource to exactly its historically observed peak removes all margin for a future spike that exceeds anything seen so far — a target band under 100% keeps deliberate headroom, which is the difference between right-sizing and over-trimming.
items.reference:
📊 Size to typical usage, not to a rare annual peak
🎯 Handle rare, known spikes deliberately and temporarily

Why: Sizing to the 99th-percentile case forever is over-provisioning with better PR.

items.prompt: In the measure -> right-size -> budget-alert -> re-audit loop, what happens if the 're-audit' step is dropped?
choices: The sizing decision quietly goes stale as usage patterns drift, the same way a one-time snapshot loses accuracy over time
Nothing changes in practice — right-sizing is a one-time exercise that only ever needs to happen once per resource
The budget alert step automatically re-triggers the measurement step on its own, so re-audit is effectively redundant
Dropping the re-audit step only affects idle/forgotten resources, not resources that have already been right-sized
items.explanation: A right-sizing decision reflects usage at the moment it was measured; without periodically re-measuring, drift in traffic, team size, or the product itself can make a once-correct sizing wrong again without anyone noticing.
items.reference:
🔁 measure → right-size → budget-alert → re-audit → (repeat)

Why: A loop only works if every step, including the repeat, actually happens.

items.prompt: Why does the right-sizing loop put 'set a budget + alert' after right-sizing rather than before it?
choices: The budget and alert are set on the new, right-sized baseline, so they reflect what spend should look like going forward rather than the old, over-provisioned number
The order is mostly a convention; the loop would work about as well with the budget-alert step placed first instead
Budgets can only meaningfully be set once, at the very start of a resource's life, and should never be adjusted afterward
Alerts must always be configured before any usage data is ever measured, since the measurement step itself technically depends on an alert already existing somewhere
items.explanation: Setting the budget and alert against the freshly right-sized baseline means the alert actually reflects the corrected, intended spend level — setting it against the old over-provisioned number would just enshrine the waste as the new normal.
items.reference:
🔁 measure → right-size → budget-alert → re-audit → (repeat)

Why: A loop only works if every step, including the repeat, actually happens.

items.prompt: According to L2's waste-pattern table, what is the recommended fix for 'idle/forgotten resources'?
choices: Tag resources with an owner and an expiry, and automate teardown or a recurring review
Delete every resource automatically after 24 hours of creation, with no owner tagging or exceptions allowed
Ban the creation of any test or staging resources entirely, so idle resources can never accumulate in the first place
Increase the overall budget enough that idle resources' ongoing cost stops being something worth tracking
items.explanation: The fix targets the actual process gap — no owner, no expiry, no recurring review — with tagging and automated or scheduled cleanup, rather than a blanket ban or simply absorbing the cost.
items.reference:
🗑️ Idle → tag owner + expiry, automate teardown
🛡️ 'Just in case' → right-size against real data, on a schedule
📈 Unbounded autoscale → explicit ceiling + alert past threshold

Why: Each pattern's fix targets its actual root cause, not just its symptom.

items.prompt: According to L2's waste-pattern table, what is the recommended fix for 'unbounded auto-scaling'?
choices: Set an explicit maximum instance count, and alert (don't just silently scale) past a threshold
Disable auto-scaling entirely and provision a fixed size forever, accepting the loss of its spike-absorbing benefit
Increase the scaling group's minimum instance count to match its maximum, so it always runs at full capacity
Nothing — unbounded auto-scaling has no real fix short of disabling auto-scaling as a pattern altogether
items.explanation: The fix keeps auto-scaling's real benefit (absorbing legitimate spikes) while adding the missing safeguard: an explicit ceiling, plus an alert when the scaling approaches it, rather than silently scaling without limit or bound.
items.reference:
🗑️ Idle → tag owner + expiry, automate teardown
🛡️ 'Just in case' → right-size against real data, on a schedule
📈 Unbounded autoscale → explicit ceiling + alert past threshold

Why: Each pattern's fix targets its actual root cause, not just its symptom.

items.prompt: L2 draws a table matching reliability-tracking concepts to cost-tracking concepts. What is the cost equivalent of an SLO?
choices: A budget — a committed spend ceiling for a period
A resource-by-resource cost dashboard, which tracks spend but without any committed target attached to it
An idle resource left running after the project that originally justified it has already ended
A right-sizing calculator, which recommends a size but doesn't commit to any spend ceiling on its own
items.explanation: Just as an SLO is a committed target on a measurable reliability signal, a budget is a committed spend ceiling on measurable cost — both turn a raw number into a decision boundary.
items.reference:
📈 SLI ↔ cost-by-resource dashboard
🎯 SLO ↔ budget
🔥 Burn-rate alert ↔ budget-forecast alert

items.prompt: What is the cost equivalent of a periodic SLO review, as this unit frames it?

Filing a recurring support ticket with the cloud provider asking them to review the account's spend
Reading the monthly invoice carefully each time it arrives, to catch drift after the fact
There is no real cost equivalent of a periodic review; cost and reliability diverge completely here
items.explanation: Just as an SLO needs periodic review as traffic patterns change, a right-sizing decision needs a periodic re-audit as usage patterns drift — both are about not letting a point-in-time decision go stale.
items.reference:
📈 SLI ↔ cost-by-resource dashboard
🎯 SLO ↔ budget
🔥 Burn-rate alert ↔ budget-forecast alert

Why: Cost needs the same signal → target → alert shape as reliability.

items.prompt: L2's worked table shows staging guessed at 4x normal load, costing about $3,600/month, versus a measured actual need of about 1.2x normal load, costing about $900/month right-sized. What does the gap between those two numbers represent?
choices: The entire waste from over-provisioning that guess — not a mistake made recklessly, but a sizing decision made once, before usage data existed, and never revisited afterward
A billing error on the cloud provider's side that needs to be formally disputed and corrected through an escalated support ticket and full account review
The genuine ongoing cost of running staging's automated test suite against a realistically-sized environment month after month
The normal, expected pricing difference between staging-tier and production-tier infrastructure that this cloud provider always charges
items.explanation: The gap between the guessed 4x sizing and the measured 1.2x actual need is exactly the waste right-sizing targets — not a reckless decision, but an unrevisited guess made before real usage data existed to check it against.

🙈 Guessed: 4x load, 16 vCPU, $3,600/mo
📏 Measured: 1.2x load, right-sized to ~$900/mo

Why: The gap between a guess and a measurement is the waste itself.

items.prompt: Why was staging's original 4x sizing never caught before the audit, even though the gap between guess and actual need was large?
choices: The sizing was set once, before any usage data existed, and nothing in the team's process ever brought someone back to check it against real measurements afterward
The team didn't have access to any monitoring tools capable of measuring staging's actual CPU or memory usage
4x normal load was actually the correct, carefully-calculated sizing, so no real gap between guess and need ever existed
Staging environments are categorically never allowed to be measured by policy, unlike production which is measured constantly and automatically by the monitoring platform
items.explanation: The original sizing decision was reasonable given the information available at the time (no usage data yet); the failure was the missing follow-up step of checking that guess against real measurements once data existed — a one-time decision with no scheduled revisit.
items.reference:
🙈 Guessed: 4x load, 16 vCPU, $3,600/mo
📏 Measured: 1.2x load, right-sized to ~$900/mo

Why: The gap between a guess and a measurement is the waste itself.

items.prompt: L2 draws a parallel between symptom-based reliability alerting and cost alerting. What is the cost-tracking analog of alerting on every single raw resource metric instead of the SLI, as infra-observability warns against?

Setting a budget so generous from the start that the forecast alert can almost never realistically fire, defeating the entire purpose of having one
Right-sizing every single resource on the exact same fixed day each month, regardless of each one's own usage pattern
There is no meaningful cost-tracking analog to alert fatigue; cost alerts don't suffer from the same noise problem

items.reference:
📈 SLI ↔ cost-by-resource dashboard
🎯 SLO ↔ budget
🔥 Burn-rate alert ↔ budget-forecast alert

Why: Cost needs the same signal → target → alert shape as reliability.

items.prompt: Why does this unit connect cost visibility so directly to infra-observability's reliability tracking, rather than treating cost as a completely separate topic?
choices: Both problems share the same underlying shape: a signal that's genuinely invisible without deliberate, proactive tracking, needing the same measure → target → alert structure to catch it before it becomes a surprise
Cost and reliability turn out to actually be the same underlying metric in disguise, just expressed in dollars instead of error rate or latency numbers
infra-observability's own monitoring tooling directly manages and silently adjusts cloud billing behind the scenes as an undocumented side effect

There's no real structural connection between the two at all; the shared vocabulary between cost and reliability tracking is purely coincidental phrasing, not a deliberate, load-bearing parallel worth drawing here
items.explanation: The structural parallel is deliberate: both cost and reliability are signals that stay invisible without deliberate tracking, and both need the same shape of fix — a measurable signal, a committed target, and a proactive alert that fires before the limit is actually breached.
items.reference:
📈 SLI ↔ cost-by-resource dashboard
🎯 SLO ↔ budget
🔥 Burn-rate alert ↔ budget-forecast alert

Why: Cost needs the same signal → target → alert shape as reliability.

items.prompt: L2 opens by asking what has to exist to catch cost creep, since nothing pages anyone the way a crash would. What's the core answer it builds toward across the level?
choices: A repeatable loop: measure real usage, right-size to it, set a budget and alert on the new baseline, and periodically re-audit as usage drifts
Hiring a dedicated finance analyst whose weekly job is reviewing invoices after they've already arrived
Setting every resource's budget to zero from the very start, so that literally nothing can ever be spent without an explicit manual approval step first
Relying on the cloud provider itself to proactively warn customers before any bill grows unexpectedly large

🔁 measure → right-size → budget-alert → re-audit → (repeat)

items.prompt: L2 emphasizes that none of L1's three decisions were individually reckless. Why does that framing matter for how a team should try to prevent future cost creep?
choices: Because the decisions were individually reasonable, prevention can't rely on catching an obviously bad call — it requires ongoing, proactive visibility that surfaces the accumulated effect, not just vigilance against obvious mistakes
It means cost creep of this particular kind is actually impossible to prevent in advance, since nobody involved ever did anything wrong at any point
It means the team should stop making any new provisioning decision at all without upfront executive sign-off required each and every time

It implies that responsibility for preventing this shifts entirely onto the finance team instead of engineering, since every one of engineering's individual provisioning decisions was reasonable at the time it was made
items.explanation: If every contributing decision looks reasonable in isolation, spotting a single obviously-bad call won't catch the problem — prevention has to come from proactive, ongoing visibility into the accumulated total, which is exactly the loop and dashboard/budget/alert structure this unit builds toward.
items.reference:
🔁 measure → right-size → budget-alert → re-audit → (repeat)

Why: A loop only works if every step, including the repeat, actually happens.

items.prompt: In `recommendSize`, why does the function take the max of peak CPU and peak memory percent as the 'binding' peak, instead of using CPU alone?
choices: A resource is only as capable as its most constrained dimension, so sizing off just CPU could ignore memory actually being closer to saturation
Memory usage is always structurally higher than CPU usage on any resource, so using CPU alone would be redundant
CPU percent isn't actually a reliably measurable quantity in most cloud monitoring systems the way memory utilization is, so it gets ignored
The choice of max over CPU alone is arbitrary, and the function could just as correctly have used CPU percent alone
items.explanation: If memory peaks higher relative to its own limits than CPU does, sizing off CPU alone would recommend a vCPU count that ignores the dimension actually closest to running out — taking the max ensures the recommendation accounts for whichever resource is the real constraint.
items.reference:
💻 bindingPeak = max(cpuPercent, memoryPercent)
🎯 impliedVcpu = currentVcpu × bindingPeak / targetBand

Why: The most constrained dimension determines real capacity, not the average of both.

items.prompt: `recommendSize` rounds `impliedVcpu` up (`Math.ceil`) rather than to the nearest whole number. Why round up specifically?
choices: Rounding down could under-provision below the calculated need, since a fraction of a vCPU isn't purchasable — rounding up guarantees at least the calculated capacity
Rounding up to the nearest whole vCPU always produces a strictly cheaper final recommendation than rounding down to that same nearest number would have produced
Math.ceil is required here specifically because the TypeScript type system rejects any fractional vCPU value passed into the function outright
It has no practical effect whatsoever on the result, since impliedVcpu's underlying calculation already always produces a whole number anyway
items.explanation: Since only whole vCPU counts are purchasable, rounding down would silently under-provision relative to the calculated target; rounding up ensures the recommendation never falls short of the number the calculation actually determined was needed.
items.reference:
💻 bindingPeak = max(cpuPercent, memoryPercent)
🎯 impliedVcpu = currentVcpu × bindingPeak / targetBand

Why: The most constrained dimension determines real capacity, not the average of both.

items.prompt: `forecastSpend` flags a resource at $8,000 of a $10,000 budget by day 10 of 30 as 'over-budget-forecast,' even though $8,000 is still technically under $10,000. Why?
choices: The straight-line daily rate ($800/day) projected to the full 30-day period forecasts $24,000, well past the budget, even though today's raw total hasn't crossed it yet
The function actually has a genuine bug here and shouldn't flag this case at all, since $8,000 hasn't technically crossed the stated $10,000 budget yet
$8,000 of spend is always treated as automatically over budget by this function, regardless of what the stated budget period actually happens to be
The forecast calculation ignores the daysElapsed parameter entirely in its formula and looks only at the raw spendSoFarUsd value passed in
items.explanation: The whole point of a forecast-based check is catching the trajectory, not just the current total — projecting the observed $800/day rate across the full 30-day period yields $24,000, 240% of budget, which is exactly the kind of early warning a spend-so-far-only check would miss.
items.reference:
📉 dailyRate = spendSoFar / daysElapsed
🔮 forecast = dailyRate × periodDays

Why: A forecast catches the trajectory before the raw total confirms the problem.

items.prompt: Why does `forecastSpend` use a straight-line daily average across the whole elapsed period, rather than only the most recent day or two?
choices: It's the simplest model, but it's slower to react to a sudden recent rate change since it dilutes a new spike with many prior lower-spend days — a trailing-window version would react faster
A straight-line average over the whole elapsed period always reacts faster to a sudden rate change than a trailing window computed over just the last couple of days would react
It's the only mathematically valid way to project future spend forward at all; any trailing-window average would be statistically incorrect by definition
The choice of averaging window has essentially no real effect on how quickly the forecast reacts to a sudden recent change in daily rate
items.explanation: Averaging over the whole elapsed period blends in many prior, lower-spend days with a sudden recent spike, so the forecast rises more slowly than the actual current rate — a trailing-window version (like a short-window burn-rate check) would surface a sudden change faster.
items.reference:
📉 dailyRate = spendSoFar / daysElapsed
🔮 forecast = dailyRate × periodDays

Why: A forecast catches the trajectory before the raw total confirms the problem.

items.prompt: What real failure can result from right-sizing a resource to its bare measured peak, with no headroom at all?
choices: A genuine traffic spike above anything previously observed can saturate the resource immediately, turning a cost fix into a real outage
The resource ends up permanently more expensive to run than it was before right-sizing was ever attempted
Right-sizing a resource to its bare measured peak has no real downside in any scenario, since the peak already represents the worst case seen
The cloud provider's API will simply reject any sizing request that's precise enough to match a measured peak exactly
items.explanation: Trimming a resource to exactly its historically observed peak removes any margin for a future spike beyond what's been measured so far — the same aggressive-trim mistake the L3 Checkpoint on the right-sizing calculator warns against.

✂️ Trim too far → no margin for a real spike → outage

items.prompt: What real failure can result from setting an auto-scaling ceiling too low purely to control cost?
choices: A legitimate traffic spike gets capped by the ceiling instead of absorbed, causing the exact reliability incident the cost guardrail was meant to prevent from happening for the wrong reason
The ceiling has no real effect on reliability at all in practice, only on the final monthly bill the team ends up having to pay
Setting any ceiling at all, however low it's set, always improves both cost and reliability simultaneously with no real trade-off involved in that decision
A low ceiling guarantees outright that the resource can never actually experience a genuine traffic spike in the first place
items.explanation: An auto-scaling ceiling set too low to control cost can turn a real, legitimate traffic spike into an outage, since the system is prevented from scaling to actually absorb the load — the cost guardrail becomes the cause of the very kind of incident reliability tracking exists to prevent.
items.reference:

🔒 Ceiling too low → legit spike gets capped → outage

items.prompt: L3 asks what changes if usage is highly seasonal (a predictable end-of-month spike) rather than steady. Why does forecastSpend's straight-line daily average handle that case poorly?
choices: It would misread a legitimate, expected spike late in the period as a budget overrun, or conversely miss that an average early-period rate understates a predictable later surge — a comparison against the same point in a typical cycle would be more accurate
Seasonal usage patterns have no real effect on forecasting accuracy at all in this model, since the daily rate always averages out any seasonal variation given enough elapsed time
forecastSpend already accounts for seasonality internally and automatically, since its periodDays parameter is specifically what captures the cyclical seasonal pattern present in the underlying data
Seasonal usage only ever affects right-sizing calculations and never touches budget forecasting at all, which is structurally immune to any seasonal usage patterns
items.explanation: A straight-line average blends a predictable seasonal pattern into a single flat rate, so it can't distinguish 'this is the expected end-of-month spike' from 'this is a genuine runaway trend' — comparing against the equivalent point in a prior, similar cycle handles that distinction the average alone cannot.
items.reference:
📅 Seasonal usage → compare to the same point in a prior cycle
👥 Shared/multi-tenant → allocate savings/spend proportionally by usage

Why: The worked example is one case, not the whole territory these tools need to cover.

items.prompt: L3 also asks what changes if the resource being right-sized is shared across five teams' workloads. Why can't the recommendSize and monthlySavings numbers be used directly by any one team in that case?
choices: The full resource's cost and savings need to be allocated back to individual teams, usually by proportional usage, before the numbers mean anything to any single team's own budget conversation
Shared resources can never meaningfully be right-sized at all under any circumstances; only single-tenant resources support this kind of calculation in practice
The calculator silently produces a completely different, mathematically incorrect formula automatically whenever a resource happens to be shared across teams
Shared resources simply have no measurable per-team utilization data to work from at all, unlike single-tenant resources which always do
items.explanation: recommendSize and monthlySavings are built assuming one team owns a resource's full cost and usage; on a shared resource, right-sizing the whole cluster is still valid, but attributing the resulting savings or overrun to a specific team requires an extra allocation step, usually proportional to each team's share of usage.
items.reference:
📅 Seasonal usage → compare to the same point in a prior cycle
👥 Shared/multi-tenant → allocate savings/spend proportionally by usage

Why: The worked example is one case, not the whole territory these tools need to cover.

items.prompt: Complete `impliedVcpu(currentVcpu, bindingPeakPercent, targetPercent)` so it returns `currentVcpu * bindingPeakPercent / targetPercent`, rounded up to the nearest whole number (never below 1). Throw an Error if `targetPercent` is not greater than 0.

tests.description: 8 vCPU, 10% peak, 65% target -> 2 vCPU (rounds up, never below 1)

items.explanation: This scales the currently-provisioned vCPU count by the ratio of the observed binding peak to the target utilization band, then rounds up (since fractional vCPUs aren't purchasable) and floors at 1 (since a recommendation of zero capacity is never valid).
items.reference:
💻 bindingPeak = max(cpuPercent, memoryPercent)
🎯 impliedVcpu = currentVcpu × bindingPeak / targetBand

Why: The most constrained dimension determines real capacity, not the average of both.

items.prompt: Complete `monthlySavings(currentVcpu, currentMonthlyCostUsd, recommendedVcpu)` so it returns the savings in dollars, rounded to 2 decimal places: cost-per-vCPU times the vCPUs removed. Throw an Error if `currentVcpu` is not greater than 0.

tests.description: recommended vCPU equal to current -> $0 saved

items.explanation: Deriving a per-vCPU cost from the current provisioning lets the savings scale linearly with however many vCPUs the recommendation removes, which is what turns a sizing recommendation into a concrete dollar figure a team can act on.
items.reference:
💰 costPerVcpu = currentCost / currentVcpu
➖ savings = (currentVcpu − recommendedVcpu) × costPerVcpu

Why: A recommendation only becomes actionable once it's translated into real dollars.

items.prompt: Complete `forecastMonthEnd(spendSoFarUsd, daysElapsed, periodDays)` so it returns the forecasted total spend for the full period, rounded to 2 decimal places: `(spendSoFarUsd / daysElapsed) * periodDays`. Throw an Error if `daysElapsed` is not greater than 0.

tests.description: $8000 spent by day 10 of a 30-day period -> $24000 forecasted
$3000 spent by day 10 of a 30-day period -> $9000 forecasted

items.explanation: Projecting the observed daily spend rate forward across the full period is what catches a bad trajectory early — waiting for spendSoFarUsd alone to exceed the budget would mean finding out only after the damage is already done.
items.reference:
📉 dailyRate = spendSoFar / daysElapsed
🔮 forecast = dailyRate × periodDays

Why: A forecast catches the trajectory before the raw total confirms the problem.

items.prompt: Complete `severityFor(percentOfBudgetForecasted)` so it returns `'over-budget-forecast'` when the forecast is 110% of budget or more, `'watch'` when it's 95% or more (but under 110%), and `'on-track'` otherwise.
items.explanation: The two thresholds separate 'trending over budget, act now' from 'trending close, worth watching' from 'currently fine' — checked from the highest threshold down so a forecast at or above 110% is never mistakenly caught by the lower 'watch' branch first.
items.reference:
✅ <95% → on-track
⚠️ 95-109% → watch
🚨 ≥110% → over-budget-forecast

Why: A tiered threshold avoids both false calm and alert fatigue.
